name: Buchdahl's Fluid Sphere
description: A static star of perfect fluid in closed form whose density falls from the centre outward and reaches zero only at infinity, so the fluid fills all of space and the mass is finite. Hans Buchdahl found it in 1964 as the relativistic counterpart of the Newtonian polytrope of index five.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A Newtonian star whose pressure grows as its density to the power $6/5$ fills all of space and still has a finite mass [buchdahl1964]. It belongs to the polytropes, stars with $p = \kappa\rho^{1+1/n}$, and its index is $n = 5$ [buchdahl1964]. Their equations of equilibrium appear to be solvable in known functions only for $n = 0$, $1$, and $5$, and from $n = 5$ up the radius is infinite, while above $5$ the mass is infinite too [buchdahl1964]. Astronomers had met it before: in 1911 H. C. Plummer set the counts of stars in globular clusters beside the density $(1 + r^2)^{-5/2}$ of a sphere of gas with $\gamma = 1.2$, a solution he credited to Schuster, and judged that the counts lend support to it [plummer1911].¶Did general relativity have a star like it? Only one polytrope was known to have an exact relativistic counterpart, the uniform sphere of $n = 0$, which is Schwarzschild's interior solution [buchdahl1964]. Hans Buchdahl found the second in 1964 [buchdahl1964]. He had come to Australia in 1940, one of the refugees from Nazi Germany whom Britain interned and shipped there on the Dunera, and in the internment camps he kept working on general relativity, writing on the only paper there was, the backs of the labels from tins of jam [melrose2012].¶He started from the outside of the star [buchdahl1964]. In isotropic coordinates Schwarzschild's vacuum is $ds^2 = -(1 - f)^2(1 + f)^{-2}c^2dt^2 + (1 + f)^4(dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2)$ with $f = GM/(2c^2r)$, which holds one constant of integration, though the field equations are of second order [buchdahl1964]. He kept that form with $f$ any function of $r$ and asked the pressure to be the same along the radius and across it, which leaves $ff'' - 3f'^2 - ff'/r = 0$; its solution $f = (a/2c^2)(1 + kr^2)^{-1/2}$ has two constants, $a$ and $k$ [buchdahl1964].¶With the mass $M$ and the length $R = k^{-1/2}$ it reads $f = GM/(2c^2\sqrt{r^2 + R^2})$, Schwarzschild's $f$ with $r^2$ raised to $r^2 + R^2$ [buchdahl1964]. Its pressure and density are positive at every radius and fall to zero only as $r$ goes to infinity, so the relativistic star has no surface either, while far out $f$ approaches $GM/(2c^2r)$ and the star weighs a finite $M$ [buchdahl1964]. Except under the most extreme central conditions its equation of state is very nearly $p \propto \rho^{6/5}$, the law of index five, and $f$ has exactly the form of the Newtonian potential of the polytrope divided by $2c^2$ [buchdahl1964]. Given the same central density and pressure, the relativistic sphere is the lighter one: when the central pressure is a third of the central energy density, its mass is $0.126$ of the Newtonian mass [buchdahl1964].¶S. Chandrasekhar had called the gravitational potential energy of the Newtonian sphere "infinite", and in 1978 Buchdahl showed that it is finite [buchdahl1978]. He had already set its finite value beside the energy of his relativistic star in 1964 [buchdahl1964]. Kjell Rosquist, looking back in 1999, counted Buchdahl's star the first physically reasonable static star to follow Schwarzschild's interior, almost half a century later, and recorded that it "was not considered to be of any significant physical interest" [rosquist1999].¶For a family of equations of state built around Buchdahl's, J. Mark Heinzle proved in 2002 that index five is a border: below it a static fluid ends at a surface, above it the fluid reaches infinity, and Buchdahl's own law is the case on the line [heinzle2002]. Lars Andersson and Annegret Burtscher called index five the borderline between finite and infinite mass and extent [andersson2019]. Takahisa Igata and Yohsuke Takamori took the sphere as a relativistic Plummer model for a dense core of dark matter and found that light can circle inside the fluid once $GM/(c^2R)$ reaches $1.3629$ [igata2022]. With Motoki Omamiuda they followed the light bent by such a core and imaged a thin disk of gas around it, keeping $GM/(c^2R)$ at or below $1.5$, where the dominant energy condition holds [igata2025].

related.text: The vacuum outside a point mass. At $R = 0$ Buchdahl's $f$ is $r_s/(4r)$, and his star is Schwarzschild's metric in isotropic coordinates [buchdahl1964].
The equations of equilibrium for a static star with any equation of state. Buchdahl's sphere solves them with an equation of state that is nearly $p \propto \rho^{6/5}$ [buchdahl1964].
The star of uniform density, the relativistic polytrope of index zero. Until 1964 it was the only polytrope known to have an exact relativistic counterpart [buchdahl1964].
Another static star of fluid in closed form whose density falls outward. Tolman's ends at a surface where the density vanishes, while Buchdahl's runs to infinity.

coordinates.name: Isotropic (Buchdahl)

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the star, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ with $M$ its mass; Buchdahl's constants are $a = GM\sqrt{k}$ and $k = 1/R^2$
Core radius, the length over which the density falls, $R = k^{-1/2}$ in Buchdahl's constants

Buchdahl's function, a pure number, largest at the centre, $f_c = r_s/(4R)$, and approaching Schwarzschild's $r_s/(4r)$ far from it; the ratio of pressure to energy density is $p/(\rho c^2) = f/(3(1 - f))$

coordinates.convention: We use Buchdahl's isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$, $r_s$ and $R$ of length; $r$ is not the areal radius, which is $r(1 + f)^2$. Components are taken in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and his signature $(+,-,-,-)$ is turned around.
